common_name: Watermelon Begonia Vine (Trailing Watermelon Begonia, Pellionia)

planting.note: Root 3-4 inch stem tip cuttings directly in moist terrarium substrate or a light, well-draining potting mix; Watermelon Begonia Vine roots readily at the leaf nodes where trailing stems touch soil, making it one of the easiest terrarium plants to propagate and fill in. Keep humidity high and temperatures above 55°F.

directions: Grow in bright indirect to medium light and high humidity — Pellionia repens is a low, creeping, succulent-stemmed groundcover from Southeast Asia in the nettle family (Urticaceae), long a staple of closed terrariums and vivariums for its speed of coverage and its fleshy, olive-green leaves with a dusty purplish-pink cast along the margins, evoking watermelon rind (hence the common name, unrelated to true begonias). The trailing stems root at every node they touch, so a single cutting will carpet a terrarium floor or spill over a pot rim within a few months. Keep the substrate evenly moist but not waterlogged; the semi-succulent stems tolerate brief dryness but stall in growth if humidity drops much below 50%. Pinch stem tips regularly to keep growth dense rather than leggy, and trim hard if it outgrows its space — it rebounds quickly from cut-back. Best used as a terrarium groundcover, hanging basket trailer, or humid-bathroom houseplant; it fades and drops leaves in dry indoor air outside an enclosure.

planting.note: Root short stem cuttings in moist terrarium substrate or a peat-based potting mix under high humidity; Satin Pellionia spreads by rooting at the nodes and fills bare terrarium floor quickly once established. Provide warmth above 60°F and avoid letting the mix dry out fully.

directions: Grow in medium to bright indirect light with consistently high humidity — direct sun bleaches the foliage and dry air causes crisping leaf edges. Pellionia pulchra is a low, mat-forming Southeast Asian groundcover closely related to P. repens but distinguished by darker, more velvety olive-green leaves overlaid with a striking network of near-black veins radiating from the midrib, giving each small leaf a quilted, satin-textured appearance that has earned it the trade name Rainbow Vine. Reddish stems creep along the substrate, rooting as they go, and knit together into a dense low carpet ideal for covering bare terrarium floor or softening the base of taller terrarium plantings. It is more particular about humidity than P. repens and sulks or drops leaves in open room air, making it best suited to closed or semi-closed terrariums, bottle gardens, and paludariums rather than open pots on a windowsill. Pinch stem tips to keep growth compact and propagate new sections easily from any rooted node.

planting.note: Root 2-3 inch stem tip cuttings in moist potting mix or terrarium substrate under high humidity; Friendship Plant roots quickly at warm temperatures (70-75°F) and benefits from frequent pinching to stay bushy rather than sprawling. Keep soil evenly moist but never soggy.

directions: Grow in bright indirect light in humus-rich, well-draining potting mix, and keep humidity elevated — this Central and South American forest-floor species (Pilea involucrata) is a compact, spreading houseplant prized for its heavily quilted, deeply veined oval leaves, which are bronzy-green above with a metallic bronze-purple sheen and deep maroon-red beneath, arranged in a low, mounding habit that thickens with regular pinching. The 'Moon Valley' cultivar, the most widely sold selection, has even more pronounced, crinkled 'moonscape' texture and chartreuse-green coloring. Friendship Plant earns its common name from how readily cuttings root and get passed between gardeners; a single stem tip roots in days under warm, humid conditions. Pinch growing tips regularly to prevent legginess, and expect stems to become woody and less attractive after 1-2 years, at which point refreshing the plant from cuttings works better than trying to rejuvenate an old specimen. Excellent in terrariums, dish gardens, and humid bathrooms; it declines quickly in dry indoor air.

planting.note: Root short stem cuttings directly in moist terrarium substrate, where they take within a week or two under warm, humid conditions; Silver Sprinkles Pilea is one of the fastest-rooting, fastest-filling terrarium groundcovers available and can overrun slower neighbors if not trimmed back.

directions: Grow in medium to bright indirect light in a light, well-draining, moisture-retentive mix — this trailing pilea (widely sold under the trade name 'Aquamarine' and often labeled Pilea glauca or Pilea glaucophylla, though its exact botanical origin remains debated among growers) produces tiny, rounded, blue-gray-green leaves with a fine silvery sheen on thin, wiry, cascading reddish stems, giving a delicate, fern-like texture reminiscent of baby tears but more drought-tolerant. It spreads quickly by rooting along trailing stems and makes an excellent low terrarium groundcover, hanging basket subject, or spiller at the edge of a mixed planter. Allow the surface to dry slightly between waterings when grown in an open pot, but keep the substrate consistently moist in a closed terrarium. Trim stems back hard whenever growth becomes sparse or leggy — it fills back in within weeks from any remaining node. Small white flowers appear sporadically but are inconspicuous; the plant is grown strictly for foliage texture.

planting.note: Divide established mats and press sections into moist, humus-rich, well-draining terrarium substrate or shallow pots; Bead Plant is shallow-rooted and spreads over the soil surface, so it establishes fastest from divided clumps rather than seed. Keep cool (55-65°F) and constantly moist for best berry production.

directions: Grow in bright indirect light with cool temperatures and constantly moist, humus-rich, well-draining substrate — Bead Plant is a mat-forming, moss-like creeper native to montane cloud forests of New Zealand, South America, and parts of Asia, grown almost entirely for its display of small, spherical, bright orange-red berries that stud the tiny leaves in autumn and winter, resembling scattered beads or coral across a low cushion of foliage. The minute, rounded, bright-green leaves on wiry, closely branched, prostrate stems form a dense, mossy mat only an inch or two tall that roots as it spreads across the soil surface. It prefers cooler conditions than most tropical terrarium plants — it struggles and declines in sustained heat above 75°F — and needs consistent moisture and high humidity to set and hold its berries; brief drying causes berry drop. Terrariums, cool greenhouses, and unheated sunrooms suit it better than warm living rooms. Often sold as a seasonal gift plant for its berry display and then kept afterward as a foliage groundcover.

planting.note: Root stem cuttings in a fast-draining, sandy potting mix; allow cut ends to callus briefly before inserting, as with most soft-succulent stems. Pussy Ears roots readily and establishes quickly in warm, bright conditions.

directions: Grow in bright indirect light to a few hours of gentle direct sun in a fast-draining, sandy or perlite-enriched mix, and allow the surface to dry between waterings — this East African semi-succulent trailer (Cyanotis somaliensis) produces fleshy, lance-shaped, silvery-green leaves densely covered in soft white hairs, giving the whole plant a fuzzy, velvety look that has earned it the common name Pussy Ears and made it a favorite for hanging baskets and terrarium edges where its texture contrasts with smooth-leaved neighbors. The trailing stems can reach a foot or more in a hanging pot and root readily wherever they touch soil. Small, vivid violet-blue three-petaled flowers appear periodically at stem tips, adding brief color to the foliage display. Unlike most fine terrarium plants, Cyanotis tolerates and even prefers drier air and soil between waterings — overwatering causes stem rot far more often than underwatering causes decline — making it a good choice for a terrarium's drier upper shelf or an open container alongside other easy-care houseplants.

common_name: Red-Edge Peperomia (Peperomia Jelly, Traffic Light Peperomia)

planting.note: Root leaf or stem cuttings in well-draining, perlite-enriched potting mix; allow cuttings to callus for a day before inserting to reduce rot risk. Red-Edge Peperomia roots slowly compared with thinner-leaved peperomias but is very reliable once established.

directions: Grow in bright indirect light in a well-draining, perlite-enriched potting mix, and allow the top half of the soil to dry before watering — Peperomia clusiifolia is a compact, upright, rosette-forming Caribbean species in the pepper family (Piperaceae) with thick, fleshy, spoon-shaped leaves in deep olive-green edged in a band of dusky red-purple, an effect most pronounced in bright light and giving rise to the trade names Red-Edge Peperomia and Peperomia 'Jelly.' The succulent leaves store water, making the plant notably more forgiving of missed waterings than thinner-leaved terrarium peperomias, though it is equally intolerant of soggy soil and prone to stem or root rot if kept wet. Its dense, low, rosette habit makes it a good structural accent among finer-textured terrarium groundcovers, and it also performs well as a compact desktop or windowsill houseplant outside an enclosure. Non-toxic to pets, unlike many common houseplants.

planting.note: Root short stem or single-node cuttings in a fast-draining, chunky mix (standard potting soil amended with extra perlite or fine bark); String of Turtles is slow to root and slow-growing overall compared with most terrarium plants, so patience is needed. Keep only lightly moist — this species is unusually prone to rot for a peperomia.

directions: Grow in bright indirect light in a very fast-draining, chunky mix, and let the soil dry substantially between light waterings — String of Turtles is a diminutive, semi-succulent, trailing Brazilian peperomia that has become one of the most sought-after small houseplants for its tiny, thick, rounded leaves patterned with dark green and silvery-gray marbling in a shape strongly resembling a miniature turtle shell, strung along thin wiry reddish stems. Despite its succulent-like water storage, the fine root system is easily damaged by overwatering, and the species is notably more rot-prone than its chunky leaves might suggest — it is generally considered a plant for growers already comfortable with succulent watering habits rather than a beginner terrarium plant. It thrives in bright light (some morning direct sun toughens growth) and appreciates a shallow, wide pot or terrarium placement with excellent drainage over a moisture-retentive but not soggy substrate. Slow-growing compared with most peperomias, it rewards patience by eventually cascading in dense strands of shell-like leaves ideal for terrarium edges, small hanging pots, or shelf displays.
